1. How to Use This Guide
Read this first - it makes every later page easier to use.
This guide helps farmers, animal health workers, students and extension staff in African countries to recognise common
diseases, pests and parasites of four livestock species and five food crops, to prevent them, and to take sensible first steps in
treatment and control. Each problem is set out in the same way: cause and spread, signs and symptoms, prevention, and
treatment and control.
Labelled diagrams. Every species and crop has a full-page diagram with numbered parts. Look at the diagram for the animal or
plant, go through each numbered part, then read the list beneath it: it tells you what an abnormal sign looks like and which
disease it may point to. Then read the matching disease entry for details.
Golden rules for farm health
 Prevention is cheaper than cure: vaccinate on schedule, control ticks, flies and worms, keep housing clean and dry, feed well,
and provide clean water.
 Isolate any sick animal or plant immediately and quarantine all new stock (animals 2-3 weeks, plants 1-2 weeks) before mixing.

officer to confirm - especially before spending money on drugs or chemicals.

 Use veterinary drugs and pesticides ONLY as the product label and a vet/extension officer direct: correct dose, correct species,
withdrawal period (animals) and pre-harvest interval (crops).
 Wear gloves, boots and a mask when handling sick animals, carcasses, pesticides or aborted material, and wash hands

1. Newcastle Disease (ND)
Viral - NOTIFIABLE - most common cause of village flock wipe-outs
CAUSE AND
SPREAD
Virulent avian paramyxovirus. Spreads by bird-to-bird contact, droplets, contaminated feed, water, cages, vehicles, shoes,
live-bird markets and apparently healthy carrier birds. Found in all African countries.
SIGNS AND
SYMPTOMS
 Sudden deaths, sometimes with no earlier signs
 Greenish, watery diarrhoea; ruffled feathers; drooping wings; sleepy, huddled birds
 Gasping, coughing, sneezing, rattling breath; swollen head and eyelids
 Nervous signs: twisted neck (torticollis), tremors, circling, walking backwards, paralysis of legs or wings
 Sudden drop in egg laying; thin-shelled, rough or misshapen eggs
 Mortality can reach 80-100 percent in unvaccinated flocks
PREVENTION
 Vaccinate: live LaSota or HB1 vaccine in drinking water or eye-drop; thermostable I-2 vaccine by eye-drop is suited to
village flocks. Repeat every 3-4 months as advised by the vet or extension officer
 Quarantine new birds for 2 weeks; do not mix species, ages or birds from markets
 Restrict visitors; footbath and handwashing at the coop door
 Clean and disinfect houses, feeders and drinkers between flocks
TREATMENT
AND CONTROL
 No cure; antibiotics only control secondary bacterial infection
 Isolate sick birds; give electrolytes and vitamins in clean water as supportive care
 Report suspected outbreaks to the District Veterinary Officer
 Bury dead birds deeply with lime or burn them; do not sell or eat sick birds
 Vaccinate healthy neighbouring birds only on veterinary advice
2. Infectious Bursal Disease (Gumboro)
Viral - affects chicks 3 to 6 weeks old
CAUSE AND
SPREAD
Birnavirus that destroys the bursa of Fabricius (the immune organ), so birds become easily infected by other diseases.
Very hardy virus that survives in houses for months; spreads by contaminated litter, equipment and people.
SIGNS AND
SYMPTOMS
 Sudden outbreak: many chicks sick within 1-2 days
 Ruffled feathers, huddling, dullness, trembling, reluctance to move
 Whitish or watery diarrhoea; soiled vent; birds peck at their own vent
 Dehydration; deaths peak on days 3-4 then fall
 Survivors are weak, stunted and have poor vaccine response (immune suppression)
PREVENTION
 Vaccinate with an intermediate Gumboro vaccine at 10-14 days, booster at 21-28 days (follow hatchery advice)
 Buy chicks from breeder flocks vaccinated so chicks have maternal antibodies
 All-in, all-out stocking; wash, disinfect and rest houses 2 weeks between batches
 Keep different ages separate
TREATMENT
AND CONTROL
 No specific treatment
 Supportive: clean water with electrolytes and glucose, vitamins A, E and K
 Keep chicks warm and reduce stress
 Antibiotics only for secondary infections, as advised by a vet

3. Fowl Pox
Viral - spread by mosquitoes
CAUSE AND
SPREAD
Avipoxvirus entering through skin wounds, mosquito and mite bites or contact. Common in the rainy season and where
there is stagnant water.
SIGNS AND
SYMPTOMS
 Dry form: wart-like, yellow then dark scabs on comb, wattles, eyelids, beak corners and unfeathered legs
 Wet (diphtheritic) form: yellow, cheesy patches in mouth, tongue, throat and windpipe
 Difficulty eating, swallowing and breathing; birds may gape
 Eyelids swell shut; reduced growth and egg production
PREVENTION
 Vaccinate by wing-web stab from 6-8 weeks, before the mosquito season; check for a 'take' (small scab) after 7-10
days
 Drain stagnant water; use mosquito control; keep houses clean and dry
 Isolate sick birds; do not mix vaccinated and unvaccinated flocks
TREATMENT
AND CONTROL
 No cure; disease runs 3-4 weeks and recovered birds are immune
 Gently remove scabs and touch lesions with iodine or antiseptic
 Vitamin A and C in water; soft food for birds with mouth lesions
 Antibiotics for secondary bacterial infections as advised by a vet
4. Marek's Disease
Viral - tumour disease of growing birds 6 to 20 weeks
CAUSE AND
SPREAD
Herpesvirus shed in feather dander and dust, carried on wind and equipment. Birds are infected as chicks but show signs
later.
SIGNS AND
SYMPTOMS
 Paralysis of one or both legs: one leg stretched forward, one backward ('doing the splits')
 Drooping wings, twisted neck, difficulty standing
 Grey or cloudy eye (grey iris) and irregular pupil; blindness
 Enlarged, hard feather follicles and skin lumps; tumours in organs
 Weight loss, pale comb, deaths
PREVENTION
 Vaccinate day-old chicks (HVT vaccine) at the hatchery - this is the only effective control
 Keep brooding chicks away from older birds; strict hygiene
 Buy from reputable hatcheries
TREATMENT
AND CONTROL
 No treatment; infected birds remain carriers
 Cull paralysed or sick birds humanely and dispose of them safely
5. Coccidiosis
Protozoal - very common in damp litter
CAUSE AND
SPREAD
Eimeria parasites in droppings. Birds swallow oocysts from contaminated litter, water and feed. Most severe in chicks 3-8
weeks old, in wet and overcrowded conditions.
SIGNS AND
SYMPTOMS
 Bloody or brown droppings (caecal form) or watery pale droppings
 Ruffled feathers, huddling, closed eyes, pale comb and wattles
 Poor appetite and thirst; weight loss; poor growth
 Pasted, dirty vents; sudden deaths in severe outbreaks
PREVENTION
 Keep litter dry; fix leaking drinkers; avoid overcrowding
 Use coccidiostat in starter feed or vaccinate (ask the feed supplier or vet)
 Clean drinkers and feeders often; rest and disinfect houses; rotate free-range yards
 Control rodents and wild birds
TREATMENT
AND CONTROL
 Amprolium or sulphonamide (e.g. sulfadimethoxine) or toltrazuril in drinking water - follow the product label and treat for
3-5 days
 Vitamin K and vitamin A to reduce bleeding and help recovery
 Replace wet litter, provide clean water and electrolytes
 Observe the withdrawal period before selling eggs or meat

6. Fowl Cholera
Bacterial (Pasteurella multocida)
CAUSE AND
SPREAD
Spread by sick birds, wild birds, rodents, contaminated water and equipment. Occurs in acute and chronic forms.
SIGNS AND
SYMPTOMS
 Acute: sudden deaths in apparently healthy birds; high fever; greenish-yellow diarrhoea
 Swollen, bluish-purple comb and wattles; laboured breathing
 Chronic: swollen wattles filled with cheesy pus, swollen joints, lameness, nasal discharge
PREVENTION
 Strict biosecurity; keep out wild birds and rodents; use clean water
 All-in, all-out production; do not add new birds to an infected flock
 Vaccinate where the disease is endemic (vaccines available from vets)
TREATMENT
AND CONTROL
 Sulphonamides or tetracyclines in water, or injectable antibiotics, as prescribed by a vet
 Cull chronic carriers; clean and disinfect the house
7. Pullorum Disease and Fowl Typhoid
Bacterial (Salmonella Pullorum / Gallinarum) - passed through eggs
CAUSE AND
SPREAD
Infected breeder hens pass Salmonella to chicks inside the egg. Also spreads through contaminated litter, feed and carrier
birds.
SIGNS AND
SYMPTOMS
 Pullorum (chicks 0-3 weeks): white chalky diarrhoea pasting the vent, huddling near heat, gasping, many deaths in the
first 2 weeks
 Fowl typhoid (older birds): pale comb, yellow-green diarrhoea, fever, thirst, loss of appetite, drop in egg production,
deaths
 Dead-in-shell embryos and weak chicks
PREVENTION
 Buy chicks from Salmonella-tested hatcheries; blood-test and cull reactor breeders
 Hygiene and disinfection; control rodents and flies
 Vaccinate against fowl typhoid where recommended (9R vaccine)
TREATMENT
AND CONTROL
 Antibiotics (sulphonamides, quinolones, etc.) reduce deaths only on a vet's prescription, but survivors stay carriers
 Cull the whole infected breeder flock where possible
8. Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza (HPAI)
Viral - NOTIFIABLE - ZOONOTIC (can infect people)
CAUSE AND
SPREAD
Influenza A virus (H5 and H7 types) introduced by wild waterfowl, live-bird trade and contaminated equipment; spreads
very fast between birds.
SIGNS AND
SYMPTOMS
 Sudden high deaths in many birds within 24-48 hours
 Swollen head and face; purple or blue comb and wattles
 Bleeding spots on the shanks (legs) and under the skin
 Respiratory distress, diarrhoea, nervous signs, sharp drop in eggs
PREVENTION
 Keep poultry away from wild birds and water bodies; cover feed and drinkers
 Do not buy birds of unknown origin; avoid sharing equipment or crates
 Wear gloves and a mask when handling sick or dead birds; wash hands thoroughly
TREATMENT
AND CONTROL
 DO NOT TREAT - report immediately to the veterinary authorities
 Authorities will cull (stamping out), disinfect and control movement
 Do not slaughter, sell or eat sick birds; do not move birds out of the area

9. External Parasites: Mites, Lice, Fleas and Scaly-leg Mite
Parasitic - common in free-range and deep-litter houses
CAUSE AND
SPREAD
Red mites hide in cracks, perches and nest boxes and bite at night; northern fowl mites and lice live on the bird; sticktight
fleas cling to the head; scaly-leg mites burrow under shank scales.
SIGNS AND
SYMPTOMS
 Restless birds at night, pale comb (anaemia), reluctance to sit in nest boxes
 Scratching, feather loss, scabs, dirty or broken feathers; lice and eggs at the feather base and vent
 Red or grey specks of mites on perches and eggs
 Scaly leg: raised, crusty, thickened scales on the shanks; lameness
 Drop in egg production and weight loss
PREVENTION
 Provide a dust-bathing area with sand and wood ash
 Seal cracks, clean and replace litter and nesting material regularly; use metal or plastic perches
 Inspect birds and perches weekly; quarantine new birds
 Do not overcrowd
TREATMENT
AND CONTROL
 Spray or dust birds and house with an approved product (e.g. permethrin or cypermethrin spray, carbaryl dust) following
the label; treat cracks and perches; repeat after 7-10 days
 Scaly leg: soak legs in warm soapy water then apply petroleum jelly, sulphur ointment or approved product
 Observe label withdrawal times for eggs and meat
10. Internal Parasites: Roundworms, Tapeworms and Gapeworm
Parasitic - worm burden is highest in free-range birds
CAUSE AND
SPREAD
Birds swallow worm eggs from contaminated soil, litter, snails, beetles or earthworms. Gapeworm (Syngamus) lives in the
windpipe.
SIGNS AND
SYMPTOMS
 Weight loss, poor growth, pale comb and wattles
 Diarrhoea, soiled vents, sometimes worms visible in droppings
 Fall in egg production
 Gapeworm: gaping, head shaking, coughing and gasping (looks like a respiratory disease)
PREVENTION
 Keep litter dry; rotate runs; separate young and old birds
 Deworm regularly (every 2-3 months for free-range flocks) and before laying
 Control intermediate hosts (snails, earthworms, beetles); clean feeders and drinkers
TREATMENT
AND CONTROL
 Piperazine, levamisole, fenbendazole or albendazole in feed or water - follow the label
 Repeat after 2-3 weeks; give vitamins to help recovery
 Observe withdrawal periods for eggs and meat

1. Peste des Petits Ruminants (PPR) - 'Goat Plague'
Viral - NOTIFIABLE - very high mortality
CAUSE AND
SPREAD
Morbillivirus of goats and sheep. Spreads by close contact, coughing and discharges, and through markets, shared water
and trade animals. Found across Africa.
SIGNS AND
SYMPTOMS
 High fever (40-41 °C), dullness, loss of appetite
 Watery then thick, sticky yellow discharge from eyes and nose, crusting and sealing the eyelids and nostrils
 Ulcers and erosions on gums, tongue and inside the lips; foul breath, drooling
 Severe, foul-smelling, watery diarrhoea and dehydration
 Coughing and rapid breathing (pneumonia); abortion; death within 5-10 days, especially in kids
PREVENTION
 Vaccinate - a single dose of live attenuated PPR vaccine gives long (often lifelong) immunity; vaccinate kids from about
3-4 months
 Quarantine new animals for 3 weeks; avoid mixing flocks at markets and water points
 Report outbreaks and restrict movements
TREATMENT
AND CONTROL
 No antiviral cure
 Supportive care: antibiotics (e.g. oxytetracycline) for secondary pneumonia, oral rehydration, clean eyes, nose and
mouth gently, good feed and shelter
 Isolate sick animals and report to veterinary services
2. Contagious Caprine Pleuropneumonia (CCPP)
Bacterial (Mycoplasma capricolum capripneumoniae)
CAUSE AND
SPREAD
Spread by coughing and close contact; a highly contagious lung disease of goats found in drier regions across Africa.
SIGNS AND
SYMPTOMS
 High fever, severe cough, rapid and painful breathing
 Standing with neck stretched, elbows out; reluctance to move
 Nasal discharge, frothy saliva; weight loss
 High deaths in adults and kids
PREVENTION
 Vaccinate (CCPP vaccine, annual) in endemic areas
 Quarantine new goats; avoid contact with infected herds and shared grazing
TREATMENT
AND CONTROL
 Early treatment: tylosin, long-acting oxytetracycline, florfenicol or tilmicosin as prescribed by a vet
 Isolate sick goats; provide shelter and clean water
 Report suspected outbreaks
3. Haemonchosis (Barber's Pole Worm) and Other Stomach Worms
Parasitic - the biggest production killer of goats in Africa
CAUSE AND
SPREAD
Worm larvae are eaten with grass. Haemonchus contortus sucks blood in the abomasum; worm eggs are passed in dung
and hatch rapidly in warm, wet weather.
SIGNS AND
SYMPTOMS
 Pale or white eyelid lining and gums (anaemia) - FAMACHA score 4-5 means treat
 'Bottle jaw': soft swelling under the lower jaw; sometimes swollen belly
 Weakness, rough coat, weight loss, poor milk production, lagging behind the herd
 Dark or scouring droppings; sudden death in kids and heavily infected animals
PREVENTION
 Use the FAMACHA eye chart to select animals for treatment (targeted selective treatment)
 Rotate grazing; do not overstock; avoid grazing very wet or short pasture; allow browsing
 Do not underdose - this builds resistance
 Quarantine and deworm new animals; use faecal egg counts to monitor
TREATMENT
AND CONTROL
 Use an effective dewormer (albendazole, fenbendazole, levamisole, closantel or ivermectin) at the correct dose for goat
bodyweight; goats usually need a higher dose than sheep or cattle of some products - check with the vet or label
 Give good protein feed, iron and vitamin B12 to anaemic animals
 Observe the milk and meat withdrawal period

4. Heartwater
Rickettsial (Ehrlichia ruminantium) - tick-borne (Amblyomma ticks)
CAUSE AND
SPREAD
Carried by bont ticks. Affects goats, sheep and cattle in many parts of Africa; new animals brought into tick areas are most
at risk.
SIGNS AND
SYMPTOMS
 Sudden high fever and loss of appetite
 Nervous signs: walking in circles, high-stepping gait, twitching eyelids, chewing movements, convulsions
 Fluid in the chest and around the heart; laboured breathing
 Sudden death, sometimes with no earlier signs
PREVENTION
 Control ticks by dipping or spraying with an approved acaricide
 Allow young animals to be infected early in tick-endemic areas where this is advised by the vet
 Be careful when introducing animals from tick-free areas
TREATMENT
AND CONTROL
 Early treatment with oxytetracycline (high dose, long-acting) as prescribed by the vet
 Supportive care; keep animals calm in shade with clean water
5. Orf (Contagious Ecthyma)
Viral - ZOONOTIC (people can catch it)
CAUSE AND
SPREAD
Parapoxvirus spreading by contact and scabs left on fences, feeding troughs and thorny browse. Common in kids and
lambs.
SIGNS AND
SYMPTOMS
 Blisters then thick, crusty scabs on lips, nostrils, muzzle and around the mouth
 Lesions on teats of does and sometimes on feet or genitals
 Kids refuse to suckle and lose weight; sore mouth
PREVENTION
 Vaccinate with live scab vaccine where available; avoid abrasive browse
 Quarantine new animals; clean, disinfect and rest contaminated pens
 Wear gloves when handling sick animals to avoid infection
TREATMENT
AND CONTROL
 Self-limiting in 2-4 weeks; no specific treatment
 Clean lesions gently with antiseptic; apply protective ointment; give soft feed
 Antibiotics for secondary infection; fly repellent on open sores
 Hand-feed kids that cannot suckle
6. Foot Rot and Foot Scald
Bacterial (Dichelobacter nodosus, Fusobacterium)
CAUSE AND
SPREAD
Occurs in wet, muddy conditions and overgrown hooves; spreads from infected hooves to others on shared soil.
SIGNS AND
SYMPTOMS
 Lameness, kneeling to graze, reluctance to walk
 Red, swollen, moist skin between toes; foul smell
 Hoof horn separates and peels away; pus under the sole
PREVENTION
 Trim hooves regularly; keep floors dry and well-drained
 Footbath (10 percent zinc sulphate) once a week during the wet season
 Quarantine and inspect feet of newly bought goats; vaccinate where available
TREATMENT
AND CONTROL
 Trim away damaged horn; clean wound
 Apply topical oxytetracycline spray or antiseptic; soak feet in zinc sulphate or copper sulphate footbath
 Injectable long-acting oxytetracycline or penicillin in severe cases (vet)
 Keep animals on clean, dry ground

A2. Goats
Educational guide - consult a vet or extension officer before treating. Follow product labels.
Page 15
7. Enterotoxaemia (Overeating Disease)
Bacterial (Clostridium perfringens types C and D)
CAUSE AND
SPREAD
Gut bacteria multiply and release toxin after a sudden change to rich feed, lush pasture or excess grain.
SIGNS AND
SYMPTOMS
 Sudden death of the best-fed, fastest-growing kids
 Abdominal pain, bloating, kicking at belly
 Profuse diarrhoea; convulsions and paddling
PREVENTION
 Vaccinate with multivalent clostridial vaccine (kids from 4-6 weeks, booster 4 weeks later; adults annually and before
kidding)
 Change feed gradually over 7-10 days; avoid overfeeding grain; feed fibre
TREATMENT
AND CONTROL
 Antitoxin and penicillin if caught early; the course is often too rapid
 Reduce feed, provide fluids, call a vet
8. Coccidiosis in Kids
Protozoal (Eimeria)
CAUSE AND
SPREAD
Kids pick up oocysts from dirty, wet, overcrowded pens and contaminated feeding areas. Most common at 3-8 weeks and
at weaning.
SIGNS AND
SYMPTOMS
 Diarrhoea (may be dark or bloody), straining, soiled tail
 Dehydration, rough coat, poor growth, weight loss
 Death in severe cases
PREVENTION
 Keep pens clean and dry; raise feeders and water troughs off the floor
 Avoid overcrowding and stress at weaning; provide coccidiostat in creep feed if advised
TREATMENT
AND CONTROL
 Amprolium, sulphonamide or toltrazuril as per label or vet
 Oral rehydration solution; separate and keep warm
9. Mange, Lice and Ticks
Parasitic - skin
CAUSE AND
SPREAD
Sarcoptes or Psoroptes mites burrow in skin; lice live in the coat; ticks feed on blood and spread disease. Spread by
contact and shared housing.
SIGNS AND
SYMPTOMS
 Intense itching and rubbing; scabs, crusts and hair loss especially on face, ears, legs, belly
 Thickened, wrinkled skin; weight loss and poor condition
 Lice: restlessness, dull coat. Ticks: visible ticks on ears, udder, groin; anaemia
PREVENTION
 Regular dipping, spraying or pour-on of the herd
 Quarantine and treat new goats; clean and disinfect housing; avoid overcrowding
TREATMENT
AND CONTROL
 Ivermectin injection (repeat after 10-14 days) or amitraz or pyrethroid sprays and washes per label
 Treat the whole herd and the pens; separate heavily infested animals
 Observe withdrawal periods for milk and meat

A2. Goats
Educational guide - consult a vet or extension officer before treating. Follow product labels.

10. Mastitis
Bacterial (Staphylococcus, Streptococcus, E. coli)
CAUSE AND
SPREAD
Bacteria enter through the teat canal from dirty bedding, unclean hands or injury.
SIGNS AND
SYMPTOMS
 Hot, swollen, hard, painful half of the udder
 Watery, clotted, bloody or yellow milk; reduced milk yield
 Fever and loss of appetite; kids refuse to suckle
 In severe cases the udder turns blue-black and cold (gangrenous mastitis)
PREVENTION
 Wash hands and udder; dry-wipe teats before milking; dip teats after milking
 Keep bedding clean and dry; milk sick animals last; dry-doe treatment
 Cull chronic cases
TREATMENT
AND CONTROL
 Strip out the affected side often; apply warm compresses
 Intramammary antibiotic infusion and injectable antibiotics as prescribed by the vet; anti-inflammatory
 Discard milk during treatment and withdrawal period
11. Brucellosis
Bacterial (Brucella melitensis) - ZOONOTIC
CAUSE AND
SPREAD
Spread through aborted foetuses, placenta, birth fluids and milk. Humans get 'Malta fever' from raw milk or contact.
SIGNS AND
SYMPTOMS
 Abortion in the last third of pregnancy; retained placenta
 Weak kids; reduced milk; swollen testicles in bucks; joint swelling and lameness
PREVENTION
 Test and cull positive animals; vaccinate kids (Rev-1) where the national programme allows
 Boil or pasteurise milk; wear gloves and boots when handling aborted material
 Isolate aborting does; dispose of foetuses and placenta safely
TREATMENT
AND CONTROL
 No practical treatment; cull infected animals under veterinary guidance
12. Bloat (Ruminal Tympany)
Metabolic - emergency
CAUSE AND
SPREAD
Gas builds up in the rumen after eating lush wet legumes, grain, or after choking.
SIGNS AND
SYMPTOMS
 Swollen left flank, distress, grunting, kicking at the belly
 Difficulty breathing, salivation; collapse and death within hours
PREVENTION
 Do not turn hungry goats onto lush legumes or wet pasture; feed dry hay first
 Introduce grain and new feeds gradually
TREATMENT
AND CONTROL
 Stand the animal with front legs raised; walk it
 Give vegetable oil or an anti-bloat drench; pass a stomach tube to release gas
 In emergencies a vet may puncture the rumen

1. African Swine Fever (ASF)
Viral - NOTIFIABLE - no vaccine or treatment (as at time of writing)
CAUSE AND
SPREAD
DNA virus that spreads by contact with sick pigs, warthogs and bushpigs, soft ticks (Ornithodoros), contaminated pork,
swill feeding, vehicles, boots and equipment. Survives long in pork and the environment.
SIGNS AND
SYMPTOMS
 High fever (40-42 °C); loss of appetite; huddling; weakness
 Red to purple blotches on ears, snout, belly, inner legs and tail
 Vomiting, bloody diarrhoea, laboured breathing, cough
 Abortion in sows; sudden deaths - mortality up to 100 percent in unvaccinated herds
 Cannot be reliably distinguished from classical swine fever without laboratory tests
PREVENTION
 Strict biosecurity: pen pigs; no free-range scavenging; fence off warthogs and bushpigs
 Never feed swill, kitchen waste or pork scraps unless boiled for 30 minutes
 Limit visitors; footbath and clean clothes; buy pigs only from known healthy sources and quarantine for 3 weeks
 Disinfect vehicles, crates and pens; control soft ticks in pens and rodents
TREATMENT
AND CONTROL
 There is no treatment or widely approved vaccine - report immediately to the veterinary authorities
 Stamping out: authorities cull infected herds, burn or deep-bury carcasses, disinfect, and enforce movement control and
a rest period before restocking
 Do not sell, slaughter, butcher or move sick pigs or pork; never dump carcasses in water or bush
2. Classical Swine Fever (Hog Cholera)
Viral - NOTIFIABLE
CAUSE AND
SPREAD
Pestivirus spread by contact, contaminated feed and equipment, and carrier pigs; looks similar to ASF.
SIGNS AND
SYMPTOMS
 High fever, huddling, loss of appetite
 Red, inflamed eyes with sticky discharge; constipation then yellow diarrhoea
 Purple blotches on skin; staggering gait; tremors in piglets
 Abortions, stillbirths; chronic wasting
PREVENTION
 Vaccinate with a licensed live vaccine where permitted; biosecurity as for ASF
 Quarantine new pigs; no swill feeding
TREATMENT
AND CONTROL
 No treatment - notify the veterinary authorities; cull and dispose of infected pigs

tuberculosis, swine erysipelas, pork tapeworm (cysticercosis) and others. Never eat or sell meat or milk from sick animals or
animals found dead; boil or pasteurise milk; cook meat thoroughly; and never open a carcass suspected of anthrax.

1. How to Use This Guide

Biosecurity and general health management
 Biosecurity checklist for any livestock farm
 Fence or house animals; control visitors, vehicles, dogs, wildlife and rodents. Provide a footbath and handwashing point at the
entrance.
 Quarantine new animals for at least 2-3 weeks and examine them before they join the herd or flock.
 Buy animals from known healthy sources, not from the nearest market where possible; avoid sharing bulls, boars, bucks or
equipment.
 Do not feed swill, kitchen waste or raw meat scraps to pigs; do not allow free-range pigs to scavenge near latrines.
 Clean and disinfect pens, houses, drinkers and feeders regularly; remove manure; keep litter and floors dry.
 Dispose of dead animals promptly by deep burial with lime or burning; do not dump carcasses in water or bush; do not skin or eat
animals found dead.
 Keep records: vaccinations, treatments, births, deaths and movements - these are useful for vets and for disease control.
 Vaccinate on schedule against the diseases present in your area, and keep vaccines cold (2-8 °C) in a cool box or refrigerator.
Responsible use of veterinary drugs and acaricides
 Use the correct dose for the animal's bodyweight and species; under-dosing builds resistance in worms, ticks and bacteria.
 Complete the course; do not share or reuse needles; observe the withdrawal period before selling milk, eggs or meat.
 Rotate classes of dewormers and acaricides; buy drugs only from registered veterinary outlets; check expiry dates and keep out
of reach of children.
 Antibiotics do not work on viral diseases (e.g. ND, PPR, ASF, FMD, LSD); they only treat secondary bacterial infection.
Safe use of pesticides and fungicides on crops
 Identify the problem first; use only products registered in your country for that crop and pest, in the label dose.
 Wear gloves, long clothing, boots, mask and eye protection; never mix or spray near water sources, food or children.
 Observe the pre-harvest interval and re-entry period; store chemicals locked away in original containers; triple-rinse and puncture
empty containers.
 Use integrated pest management (IPM): resistant varieties, crop rotation, clean seed, field hygiene, traps, natural enemies and
botanicals such as neem, with chemicals only when needed.

What to do in a suspected disease outbreak (livestock)
 1. Isolate sick animals at once and stop all movement of animals, products and people in and out of the farm.
 2. Call your vet or District Veterinary Officer; give number sick and dead, species, age, signs and recent movements.
 3. Do not slaughter, sell or eat sick animals or animals that die suddenly; do not move carcasses.
 4. Wear gloves and boots; wash and disinfect hands, boots, equipment and vehicles after contact.
 5. Dispose of carcasses by deep burial with lime or burning, as directed by officials.
 6. Follow official orders on quarantine, vaccination and compensation; restock only after cleaning and the recommended rest
period.
What to do in a suspected crop disease or pest outbreak
 1. Walk the field in a zig-zag and record how many plants are affected and which parts (leaf, stem, root, fruit, grain).
 2. Take a sample (whole plant with roots, wrapped in damp paper) to the extension officer or plant clinic; photograph symptoms.
 3. Remove and destroy badly infected plants; do not compost diseased material.
 4. Choose control according to the cause: fungicide for fungi, bactericide or hygiene for bacteria, vector control for viruses,
insecticide or biocontrol for insects.
 5. Clean tools, boots and wheelbarrows between fields; plan crop rotation and resistant varieties for the next season.

A1. Chickens (Poultry)
Most village flocks are free-range and unvaccinated. Newcastle disease, parasites and predators are the leading causes of
loss.
Highly contagious; pigs spread huge amounts of virus. See also the cattle section.
SIGNS AND
SYMPTOMS
 Fever; blisters on the snout, tongue, lips, coronary band and between the toes, and on the teats
 Severe lameness; pigs refuse to stand; hooves may be lost
 Piglets can die suddenly
PREVENTION
 Vaccinate with a vaccine matching local serotypes; restrict movement and visitors
 Do not feed untreated waste from infected areas
TREATMENT
AND CONTROL
 No specific treatment; supportive care and soft bedding
 Report to authorities; isolate and follow official control instructions

4. Swine Erysipelas
Bacterial (Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae) - ZOONOTIC
CAUSE AND
SPREAD
Bacteria live in soil and on tonsils of healthy pigs; outbreaks follow stress, weather changes or poor hygiene.
SIGNS AND
SYMPTOMS
 Sudden fever (41 °C), stiffness, reluctance to move
 Raised, red or purple diamond-shaped skin patches on the back, sides and neck
 Swollen painful joints (chronic arthritis); abortion; sudden death
PREVENTION
 Vaccinate breeding stock and growers as per vet schedule
 Keep pens clean; control rodents; reduce stress
TREATMENT
AND CONTROL
 Penicillin early, as prescribed by the vet; anti-inflammatory for fever
 People: wear gloves; the infection can cause skin lesions (erysipeloid) in humans
5. Internal Parasites: Ascaris, Nodular Worm and Others
Parasitic
CAUSE AND
SPREAD
Eggs passed in dung survive for months in pens and soil; pigs swallow them from contaminated floors, feed and water.
Free-range and wet pens have the highest worm burden.
SIGNS AND
SYMPTOMS
 Poor growth and feed efficiency, pot belly, rough coat
 Coughing ('thumps') when larvae migrate through the lungs
 Diarrhoea; worms visible in dung; 'milk spot' liver damage at slaughter
PREVENTION
 Wash sows before farrowing; clean and dry pens; do not overstock
 Deworm sows 1-2 weeks before farrowing, piglets at weaning, and growers every 2-3 months
 Rotate pastures for outdoor pigs
TREATMENT
AND CONTROL
 Ivermectin, fenbendazole, albendazole or levamisole as per label; repeat as directed
 Observe withdrawal period before slaughter
6. Mange and Lice
Parasitic - skin
CAUSE AND
SPREAD
Sarcoptes scabiei mites burrow in skin; spread from sow to piglets and between pigs in contact; lice live on skin folds.
SIGNS AND
SYMPTOMS
 Intense itching; rubbing on walls and posts
 Scabs and thickened, crusty skin on ears, flanks, legs and belly; hair loss
 Reduced growth and appetite; sows scratching
PREVENTION
 Treat sows before farrowing; treat new pigs on arrival
 Clean and disinfect pens; avoid overcrowding
TREATMENT
AND CONTROL
 Ivermectin injection (repeat in 10-14 days) or amitraz wash/spray per label
 Treat the whole herd and the pens
 Observe withdrawal periods
7. Porcine Cysticercosis (Pork Measles)
Parasitic (Taenia solium) - ZOONOTIC - public health danger
CAUSE AND
SPREAD
Pigs eat human faeces containing tapeworm eggs when free-ranging near homes. Cysts develop in pig muscle and
tongue. People eating undercooked infected pork get tapeworms; eggs shed by carriers can cause neurocysticercosis
(epilepsy) in humans.
SIGNS AND
SYMPTOMS
 Pigs usually look healthy
 Small white cysts (measles) in the tongue, meat and heart; cysts may be felt under the tongue
 Discovered at slaughter or meat inspection
PREVENTION
 Build and use latrines; keep pigs penned, not free-roaming
 Cook pork thoroughly; condemn infected carcasses at meat inspection
 Treat people with tapeworms; community health education
TREATMENT
AND CONTROL
 Oxfendazole may be used in pigs under vet advice, but carcasses of infected pigs must not be eaten
 Human carriers are treated by health workers (e.g. niclosamide or praziquantel)

8. Neonatal and Post-weaning Diarrhoea (E. coli Scours)
Bacterial
CAUSE AND
SPREAD
Piglets pick up E. coli from dirty farrowing pens, udders and floors; cold, damp pens and poor colostrum intake increase
risk.
SIGNS AND
SYMPTOMS
 Watery yellow, white or grey diarrhoea; wet, dirty rear end; strong odour
 Dehydration, sunken eyes, shivering; piglets lose weight and die
 Post-weaning: scours, poor growth, swollen eyelids (oedema disease)
PREVENTION
 Clean and disinfect farrowing pens; wash sows before farrowing
 Ensure piglets suckle colostrum within hours of birth
 Keep the piglet nest warm (about 30-35 °C), dry and draught-free
 Vaccinate sows where available; avoid sudden weaning feed changes
TREATMENT
AND CONTROL
 Oral rehydration solution and warmth
 Antibiotics chosen by the vet (preferably after sensitivity testing)
 Keep sick piglets separate and pens clean
9. Piglet Anaemia (Iron Deficiency)
Nutritional
CAUSE AND
SPREAD
Sow milk is low in iron; piglets on concrete floors cannot get iron from soil.
SIGNS AND
SYMPTOMS
 Pale skin, wrinkled hairless skin; poor growth at 1-3 weeks
 Rapid, laboured breathing ('thumping'); weak piglets; sudden death
PREVENTION
 Inject iron dextran as per label within the first 3 days of birth; repeat if advised
 Provide clean iron-rich supplements or a sod of clean soil in concrete pens
TREATMENT
AND CONTROL
 Iron injection and good nutrition; treat the sow and piglets as per vet advice
10. Swine Pneumonia (Mycoplasma and Bacterial)
Bacterial
CAUSE AND
SPREAD
Spread by coughing and nose-to-nose contact; worsened by cold, damp, poor ventilation, overcrowding and dust.
SIGNS AND
SYMPTOMS
 Dry or moist cough; fever; laboured, abdominal breathing
 Poor growth, dullness, reduced appetite; sometimes sudden deaths
PREVENTION
 Good ventilation, avoid draughts and overcrowding; all-in, all-out
 Vaccinate against Mycoplasma and bacteria where advised; quarantine new pigs
TREATMENT
AND CONTROL
 Antibiotics prescribed by a vet (e.g. tylosin, tetracyclines, florfenicol)
 Isolate sick pigs; give warmth and fresh air

Swollen left flank (bloat); sunken flank (not eating); pot belly (worms)

Hot hard quarter, clots in milk (mastitis); blisters (FMD); ticks on udder
11

Soiled with diarrhoea or blood; ticks under the tail; aborted foetus discharge

Lameness, swollen joints, foot lesions; blackleg swelling in thigh
